text: Following the RNN experiments, we explored pretrained Transformers to improve reply generation (Vaswani et al., 2017). V5 aimed to produce a relevant Standard English reply and a natural Singlish version with the same meaning. We began with mT5-base before exploring larger models.

We selected mT5-base, a multilingual encoder–decoder model with approximately 582 million parameters (Xue et al., 2021). Training had two main stages: language and conversation adaptation, followed by project-specific reply training. An initial span-corruption phase, recorded as Stage 0 in the code, formed part of language adaptation.

text: LoRA reduced the number of parameters updated during task training (Hu et al., 2021). However, independently generating the two styles often changed the reply’s meaning. For example, one version could agree while the other refused, or confuse who should lend an item.

We changed the pipeline to generate an English reply first, then rewrite that exact draft into Singlish. Both tasks used the same mT5 adapter with different task prefixes. This improved consistency between the two outputs, although an incorrect English reply could still lead to an incorrect Singlish reply.
Figure 3.3a placeholder — English-first pipeline: conversation → English draft → Singlish rewrite. Show the same intended meaning across both outputs.
We also tested several ways to improve contextual understanding. These produced useful changes in individual cases, but no consistent overall improvement over the stronger mT5 reference.

text: We next explored SEA-LION-v1-3B, a decoder-only model pretrained on Southeast Asian languages (AI Singapore, n.d.). Its replies were generally more coherent and useful in the conversations reviewed. We retained the English-first approach, using separate English and Singlish adapters. Public-dialogue adaptation was followed by project-specific LoRA training; the final settings are summarized in Section 3.5.

We preferred four-beam search over greedy decoding because it produced cleaner, more complete replies in reviewed examples. The selected pipeline blocked repeated three-grams and allowed up to 64 generated tokens per reply.

Qwen2.5-3B was also explored as a similarly sized alternative (Qwen Team, n.d.). It produced coherent replies, suggesting that general conversational ability was important alongside regional-language exposure. Our validation inputs were mainly English-based chats with light Singlish: 30/50 listed local terms, while only 2/50 carried a pinyin tag. This gives limited evidence about extended code-switching, rather than showing that regional understanding is unimportant.
Figure 3.3b placeholder — One shared conversation with mT5, SEA-LION and Qwen replies side by side. Highlight relevance and English–Singlish meaning consistency.

Validation loss was used to select checkpoints within a training setup, rather than rank different model families. A fair model comparison should use the same conversations, judge settings and criteria: appropriateness, naturalness and style fit, with a separate check of English–Singlish meaning. The exploratory observations here are qualitative; the model variants still require matched re-evaluation.

SEA-LION was selected as the V5 generator for its balance of coherent replies and local phrasing. The shared system evaluation uses Gemma 12B as the judge and is reported in Section 4. Qwen’s separate role in reranking and local-wording refinement is described in Section 3.4.
